column3: It supplies the preceding statement of the Romans' defeat, the starting state that the focus immediately reverses.
Reviving the earth after its death offers a distinct created-sign pattern of reversal after an apparently settled state.
It treats victory and death as outcomes under God's reward, adding a broader frame in which dominance is not self-determining.
God's help makes a people dominant, directly supporting the focus's movement from defeat to victory, though it is less specific.
The next ayah names this coming reversal as God's promise, directly securing the focus's future-tense declaration.
Its true divine promise and warning against worldly deception only loosely support the focus's contrast between present appearance and future outcome.
The promise that God's forces will be dominant reinforces divinely given victory, but repeats the same core point after closer cards.
Succession after a former people gives a remote social instance of changed position rather than the focus's announced military reversal.
Its use of nearness concerns accessible garden fruit and does not clarify the focus's low or nearby land.
The righteous inheriting the earth supplies a broader land-possession reversal, though without the focus's defeat-and-victory sequence.
Its creation and return pattern continues the surah's ordered transformations but does not explain the Romans' reversal.
Settlement in the land after oppressors offers a distant replacement pattern, constrained by fear of God and His warning.
Its use of adna concerns legal testimony and does not add to the focus's place or reversal.
God's aid and mercy directly identify the agency behind the victory announced in the focus.
The vision of heavenly and earthly dominion does not materially clarify defeat, later victory, or the specified land.
Passing by signs in heaven and earth does not illuminate the focus's temporal reversal.
The exposure of disputed truth and the deniers' falsehood develops the certainty of a promised future event.
Spreading out the earth shares only the land term and adds no relevant account of reversal or dominance.
It explicitly makes overcoming or being overcome depend on divine help, usefully framing the focus's predicted victory.
The liturgical times continue the surah's measured order but add little to the specific defeat-to-victory announcement.
Earth revived after death is another reversal image, but it is redundant after the earlier comparable card and remains distinct in scene.
Its use of adna concerns avoiding financial burden in marriage, not the focus's place or victory.
The bounded span of years and God's command before and after directly complete the focus's predicted reversal.
Universal lordship of heaven and earth does not add a focused account of the Romans' changing condition.
Its use of adna counts private conversations and is unrelated to the focus's near or low land.
The question about being granted delay faintly relates to time before a promised outcome, but adds little.
Creator names and universal praise do not clarify the focus's reversal of power.
Universal prostration gives no specific contribution to defeat, victory, or the land setting.
Praise across heaven, earth, and daily times maintains the surah's ordered frame but is not specific to the announced reversal.
The earth's crushing is a judgment scene without a meaningful link to the focus's defeat and later victory.
Deliberate distortion after understanding does not clarify the focus's temporal claim.
Creation's diversity is nearby surah context but does not add to the change from defeat to victory.
Its warning about advocacy on the Day of Judgment is unrelated to the focus's political reversal.
It mentions an unattained aim and painful punishment, offering only a distant contrast to the focus's future success.
Extended enjoyment over years lightly resonates with the focus's bounded future interval but does not explain it.
Divine administration from heaven to earth and measured time offer a broad temporal-order frame, without the focus's reversal.
The judgment scene and failed ransom do not materially illuminate the focus.
Life, death, and revival continue the surah's reversal imagery, but remain a distinct natural and eschatological pattern.
God's written declaration that He and His messengers will prevail directly reinforces victory as a settled divine determination.
Dispute about marching toward death does not clarify the focus's predicted dominance.
The surah's appeal to earlier, stronger peoples whose end can be inspected gives historical perspective against treating present power as permanent.
Dense gardens share a root form only and do not clarify being overcome or later overcoming.
Its use of adna measures part of the night and offers no focused contribution to the land or reversal.
The arrival of what had been promised reinforces eventual fulfillment, though it is now largely covered by closer promise cards.
God's possession of heaven and earth does not specifically illuminate the focus's sequence of defeat and victory.
The contrast between lower and better provisions gives a lexical echo of adna but belongs to a different evaluative setting.
The criminals' despair at the Hour continues the surah's future horizon but adds little to the focus's historical prediction.
Lordship of heaven, earth, and what lies between does not add to the focus's reversal.
The imagined ransom by everyone on earth is unrelated to the focus's land and victory claim.
The surah's assertion of creation in truth and for an appointed term supports a world governed by fixed purpose and time.
The call to believe God's signs after His recitation does not clarify the focus's announced event.
Making later people successors in the earth offers a broad post-predecessor pattern, but not the focus's conflict reversal.
An inescapable appointment and removal from contact faintly support the theme of fixed outcomes, in a different scene.
It joins being overcome to final gathering, a punitive contrast that does not explain the focus's promised recovery.
Corruption in the earth has no material link to the focus's reversal of dominance.
The failure of alleged partners to intercede is nearby eschatological context, not an explanation of the Romans' future victory.
Following whichever side proves dominant shows a contingent human response to victory, but adds little after direct dominance cards.
The question about earth-origin gods reviving the dead does not clarify the focus.
Universal obedience to God does not add a specific account of defeat becoming victory.
The earth's breadth as a field for faithful movement is a distinct use of land, not the focus's location or reversal.
The heaven and earth not mourning a destroyed people does not clarify the focus's promised military change.
It concludes that prolonged enjoyment did not benefit them, a limited warning against reading present condition as final.
The nearer and greater punishments offer a different graded use of adna, with little help for the focus's geographic or temporal claim.
Its use of adna measures nearness in a vision and does not clarify the focus's land.
The separation at the Hour continues the surah's future sequence but does not add to the bounded victory prediction.
The brothers' imagined righteousness after wrongdoing is a temporal self-justification, only distantly comparable to change after an act.
Earlier stronger peoples and their observed end reinforce that strength is not permanent, though this repeats the closer surah example.
The irreversible day and division extend the surah's fixed-outcome pattern, but not the focus's historical reversal.
Seeking reward for victory illustrates an interested relation to dominance, without explaining its reversal in the focus.
It corrects a boast that the mighty will expel the lowly by locating true might with God, a pointed counter to human claims of dominance.
The believers' joy in a garden supplies the positive outcome within the surah, but it is not the joy over the focus's victory.
It denies escape from God anywhere on earth, a broad sovereignty claim that only indirectly frames the land setting.
God's promise to grant succession, establishment, and security after fear gives a close social pattern of divinely ordered change in condition.
The command to inspect former peoples' ends strengthens the surah's warning that present earthly strength is historically reversible.
Cosmic upheaval of earth and mountains does not clarify the focus's historical defeat and later victory.
God's promise of one group and His purpose to establish truth show victory unfolding through a divine intention beyond immediate preference.
The sworn denial and God's binding promise of resurrection reinforce the reliability of a future claim despite present disbelief.
The prayer for worldly and final good and protection from the Fire does not add to the focus's announced reversal.
Long enjoyment is set against a shrinking earthly reach, then asks whether they can be dominant, directly challenging apparent lasting power.
Those who deny the signs and the Hereafter being brought to punishment complete the surah's consequence sequence but not the focus's reversal.
The earth being spread out is an eschatological scene unrelated to the focus's near or low land.
Succession in the land after Aad gives another replacement pattern, but it is less direct and redundant after similar cards.
Human joy at mercy and despair at adversity develops unstable responses to changing circumstances, not the focus's promised reversal itself.
Alliances and corruption on earth do not clarify defeat turning into victory.
Broken covenant and the evil abode give a broad consequence for corruption, without a useful link to the focus's specific event.
Worldly idol bonds breaking at judgment does not clarify the focus's temporal reversal.
The rhetorical question about belief after this message does not add to the focus.
Later successors choosing the lower worldly gain despite the better Hereafter give a remote adna contrast, not the focus's reversal.
The opening letters do not independently clarify the focus ayah.
The would-be victors are overcome and reduced in the same setting, a vivid concrete reversal of dominance.
Its strong community image and promised reward offer only an indirect collective-success resonance.
Punishment for harming God and His messenger does not add to the focus's place or reversal.
The earth's fissures do not materially clarify the focus's near or low land.
Travel through the earth to observe creation and later origination gives a broad investigative use of land, not the focus's event.
The lost say their wretchedness overcame them, a contrasting use of overcoming that adds little after direct victory reversals.
God's ownership of heaven and earth and exalted greatness do not clarify the focus.
Enduring punishment in Jahannam is a fixed adverse condition, only remotely contrasting with the focus's promised altered condition.
The prohibition on arrogant walking on earth does not clarify the focus's land or change in dominance.
The mention of a group from earlier people has no material relation to the focus.
God's dominion over heaven and earth is too general to add to the focus's defeat-to-victory claim.
It explicitly gives and removes dominion and exalts and abases whom God wills, furnishing the clearest general account of power as reversible rather than inherent.
God's help at Badr while the believers were weak provides a concrete precedent for victory that reverses an unfavorable visible condition.
Its assurance of eventual superiority to believers directly counters reading a present setback as a final status.
The statement that none can alter God's words, followed by help reaching earlier messengers, reinforces the reliability of the promised reversal.
The good word is fulfilled for the patient oppressed, who inherit eastern and western lands after Pharaoh's power is destroyed; this is a close historical reversal of dominance.
Divine aid is made good news and reassurance, while victory is located with God alone, directly explaining the agency of the focus's future overcoming.
The command about a small steadfast group overcoming a larger one gives a battlefield instance in which numerical appearance does not settle the outcome.
It again describes a smaller patient force overcoming a larger one by God's permission, adding a concrete proportional reversal.
God promises punishment through the believers' hands, victory over opponents, and healing for believers, directly linking divine action to an altered conflict outcome.
When apparent support collapses, God aids His messenger and makes the disbelievers' word lowest while God's word is highest, strongly framing true dominance.
God's established way of saving messengers and believers after danger gives a direct prophetic pattern for the rescue and reversal announced in the focus.
God does not change a people's condition until they change what is within themselves, supplying a broader principle of altered collective condition.
It presents a historical sequence in which one group gains entry and triumph after prior corruption, a consequential though distinct reversal of power.
God's promise to help those who help His cause directly states the divine support that makes a later victory possible.
The same surah explicitly says earlier messengers brought proofs and were avenged against criminals, and that helping believers is incumbent upon God; it is the closest omitted surah parallel.
The command to observe how God revives the earth after its death offers the surah's own visible sign that a lifeless state is not final.
Creation through weakness, strength, then weakness and grayness presents changing condition as an ordered divine succession rather than a fixed essence.
It commands patience because God's promise is true, directly answering how the focus's future declaration should be held amid present appearance.
God declares His help for messengers and believers in worldly life and when witnesses stand, a direct general counterpart to the focus's promised victory.
The reciprocal promise that God will help believers and make their footing firm gives a concise mechanism for overcoming after instability.
The declaration of a clear victory is a direct instance of the divine bestowal of victory central to the focus.
It explicitly pairs the messenger with mighty divine help, reinforcing victory as aid rather than autonomous power.
God's purpose to make His religion prevail over all religion offers a broader, programmatic statement of divinely effected predominance.
The promise of help from God and a near victory directly joins divine aid, imminence, and victory in a way especially relevant to the focus.
The arrival of God's help and victory supplies a succinct later realization of victory as a divine arrival rather than a permanent human possession.
